chunks: And from him, from several of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah, from his father, from Abdillah ibn al-Fadl, from al-Nawfali, from his father, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

He was asked about the beggar who asks but it is not known what his need is, so he said: 'Give to the one whom mercy falls upon in your heart.' And he said: 'Give less than a dirham.' I said: 'What is the maximum that is given?' He said: 'Four qirats (dawaneeq).'

key_terms.الدِّرْهَمُ: A silver coin, used here as a unit of currency
key_terms.دَوَانِيقَ: Plural of daniq, a small copper coin; four dawaneeq equal one dirham

ai.seo_question: What is the maximum amount of charity to give to a beggar when their specific need is unknown according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) addresses the practical challenge of zakat distribution to unknown recipients by prioritizing the giver's intuitive mercy (*rahma*) over rigid verification. He sets a specific upper limit of four dawaneeq (approximately one dirham) to prevent excessive giving that might encourage dependency or laziness, reflecting the Shia scholarly emphasis on balancing generosity with fiscal prudence in communal welfare.
